summary: Presents a few observations on NCP statistics, with measured distributions of NCP message types and IMP message types.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 618 presents operating statistics from the NCP at Harvard and draws several possible conclusions from them. The author discusses delayed RFNMs, allocation traffic and the number of NOP messages.

questions: what did rfc 618 observe in ncp statistics
subtitle: Observations from NCP and IMP statistics collected at Harvard.

tldr.problem: The author wanted NCP implementers to consider what operating and error statistics from a live system could reveal about message timing and allocation strategies.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC presents Harvard NCP and IMP counts collected since the system restart, including message types, errors, RFNMs and data-message sizes.
tldr.outcome: The author suggests that some discarded RFNMs may have been delayed beyond the timeout, and describes an allocation strategy intended to reduce control traffic for small messages.

facts.label: NCP timeout the author believed applied

today: RFC 618 is a 1974 report of NCP and IMP statistics and the author's observations about them.

sections.title: Statistics from a Running NCP
sections.content: The NCP at HARV-10, CMU-10A and CMU-10B collected operating and error statistics that a user could display with the IMP ERROR command. The figures covered time since the last restart and were not stored permanently. The sample output in this RFC was collected after 168 hours of uptime.
sections.plainLanguage: The NCP kept counts of messages and errors that a user could display on request. The example covers the period since the system restart and was collected after 168 hours.

sections.title: RFNMs and Allocation Strategy
sections.content:
The author observes that discarded unexpected RFNMs equaled simulated, timed-out RFNMs in the sample, and says this pattern occurred often. He suggests that RFNMs might be delayed beyond the timeout, which he believed was 30 seconds, rather than lost, and raises longer timeouts as a possibility.

The sample also showed about twice as many received allocates as transmitted allocates. The author describes the Harvard NCP's strategy: each socket has a desired allocation level, and when actual allocation falls below 50% of that level, the NCP sends enough to restore the desired level. He says this reduces allocate traffic for small messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The author suggests some RFNMs counted as discarded may have arrived too late. He also describes how the Harvard NCP sent allocation updates in groups instead of after every small message.

sections.title: NOP Messages and Other Counts
sections.content:
The author notes that NOPs were about 25% of received control messages, although most appeared to be carried along with other control messages. The sample output includes message-type totals, IMP faults, RFNM counts, a histogram of data-message sizes, 72 free buffers and 7% average buffer utilization.

The RFC presents these figures as observations for NCP implementers, not as measurements of every network site.
sections.plainLanguage: The sample showed many NOP messages, but the author says most were piggy-backed on other control messages. The report also includes buffer-use and message-size counts.
